episodes.214557: Numerous thunderstorms tracked northeast across eastern Colorado. A few of these thunderstorms produce severe wind gusts. The strongest being an 82 mph wind gust near Sterling.
episodes.214585: Thunderstorms produced strong winds across the bays and Gulf waters.
episodes.214586: Thunderstorms produced strong winds and isolated damage across the area.
episodes.214587: Thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall which resulted in flash flooding in Southwest Houston and Sugar Land.
episodes.214717: Despite upper-level ridging over the region, a weak disturbance in the flow aloft and differential heating led to isolated shower and thunderstorm development over the Permian Basin. Storms were short-lived, but dry low-levels allowed for a downburst to occur in Odessa.
episodes.214736: A lingering cold front resulted in scattered severe thunderstorms from east-central Virginia to southern Maryland during the late afternoon to mid evening hours.
episodes.215769: Heavy rainfall over NW El Paso County led to some minor, localized street flooding. One report of stranded vehicles and water flowing over the road occurred south of the U.S. Air Force Academy.
episodes.215772: A cold front located in the Triad region of North Carolina on the morning of July twenty-third tracked east through the morning hours eventually stalling across the inland rivers and sounds of Eastern North Carolina during the afternoon hours. Along and out ahead of this front a line of ongoing showers and thunderstorms tracked east as well. A few of these storms became strong to severe in nature with strong wind gusts being the primary hazard in the strongest storms.
episodes.216189: A southward moving cold front gradually moved south during the early morning to early evening hours. As that happened, waves of showers and storms tracked along and south of the front. This led to a few isolated flash flooding reports over the Triangle and Sandhills of central North Carolina.
episodes.216402: The nearly stationary front that produced flash flood north of the Knoxville metro area on the 22nd, moved slowly southward on the 23rd. Another round of training thunderstorms and heavy rains produced some isolated flash flooding in Monroe county during the morning hours of Thursday the 23rd.
episodes.216507: A shortwave moved across Wyoming and triggering numerous thunderstorms.
episodes.216617: During the late evening hours on the 22nd, a cluster of seemingly weak showers and thunderstorms from a radar standpoint moved northeast across portions of east-central Colorado. A measured wind gust of 64 mph occurred in Cheyenne County.
episodes.216660: Slow-moving and training showers and storms produced heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding across northeast North Carolina during the early morning hours of July 23.
episodes.216809: Slow-moving and training showers and storms produced heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding across the urban corridor of southeast Virginia during the early morning hours of July 23.
episodes.217474: Early in the evening on July 23rd, a broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across much of southwest Kansas within a hot, humid surface environment. Thunderstorms moved east in an environment with mid to upper 60s dewpoints and southeasterly surface winds. High temperature-dewpoint spreads and fairly weak mid and upper level winds favored damaging wind gusts as the primary mode of severe weather with these storms. The storms were strongest as the moved across the U.S. Highway 83 corridor of Finney and Haskell County.
episodes.217494: A strong low-pressure system originating in the Bering Sea moved across mainland Alaska in mid-to-late July 2026, bringing multiple rounds of anomalous, heavy rainfall to Southcentral Alaska that approached record levels for the month. Between July 13 and July 23, persistent wet conditions saturated the region, with the heaviest precipitation focused over the Talkeetna Mountains and the Susitna Valley. The Talkeetna River Basin received 4 to 6 inches of rain, or a 5- to 10-year average recurrence interval. Meanwhile the Yentna Basin saw 10-day totals of 6 to 8 inches. This excessive runoff caused fast-responding rivers and streams to swell, leading to moderate flooding, severe riverbank erosion, road washouts, and a local emergency disaster declaration by the Matanuska-Susitna Borough Assembly.

Heavy rainfall caused Moose Creek to rise rapidly, surpassing the minor flood stage of 16.5 feet on the Moose Creek at Oilwell Road stream gage. By the morning of July 23, the river stage reached 16.55 feet, and an estimated 1.5 feet of water was flowing over Oilwell Road due to a culvert issue, rendering the road impassable for cars and blocking access to the stream gage. Water levels on Moose Creek were the highest recorded since 2006. By 11:00 AM on July 24, water levels had receded enough for vehicles to travel the road again, though an observer reported that approximately 60 feet of the road surface on the southwest approach to the bridge remained flooded into the late afternoon.   The flooding was driven by localized heavy rainfall, with three-day totals varying between 2.90 inches at the Tokositna Snotel site and 3.59 inches at Talkeetna.

Several rounds of heavy rain resulted in moderate flooding and severe, accelerated riverbank erosion in Talkeetna, prompting a preemptive local emergency disaster declaration by the Mat-Su Borough Assembly. Rapid bank erosion threatened approximately eight riverfront structures, including four primary residences and two businesses, leaving one residence in imminent danger of collapsing into the river. An outbuilding was lost, and approximately 30 feet of bank washed away near Susitna River Lodging within a 48-hour period. Significant erosion also destroyed approximately 40 feet of the BLM runway, while floodwaters inundated areas near Main Street and forced the borough to close the Talkeetna River campground. Further damage included road washouts along Cummings and Beaver Roads, and a landslide that halted Alaska Railroad service north of the town. The flooding was driven by 4 to 6 inches of rainfall concentrated over the Talkeetna Mountains between July 19 and July 23. This produced a crest of 13.07 feet on the upstream Talkeetna River gage (TRTA2), 14.25 feet at the Talkeetna River railroad bridge gage (TKTA2), and 24.20 feet on the Susitna River (SUNA2).
